desc:
You own counts[i] coins of value coins[i] (all values distinct). Count the different ways to choose some of these coins so that their total is exactly amount.

Two ways are different if some value is used a different number of times; coins of equal value are interchangeable. Return the count modulo 1,000,000,007. Choosing no coins is one way to make an amount of 0.

coins = [1,2,5], counts = [2,2,1], amount = 6 -> 2   (5+1 and 2+2+1+1)
coins = [1,5],   counts = [3,1],   amount = 5 -> 1   (just the 5)
coins = [4],     counts = [1],     amount = 8 -> 0
constraints: 1 ≤ coins[i] ≤ 1,000 and all values are distinct
hints: Process one value at a time. Let ways[s] be the number of ways to make s with the values handled so far.
For a new value c with count k, new[s] = ways[s] + ways[s - c] + ... + ways[s - k*c]: you decide how many copies j (0..k) to take. Summing up to k terms for every s is too slow if done naively.
That sum is a sliding window over positions s, s - c, s - 2c, .... Use new[s] = new[s - c] + ways[s] - ways[s - (k + 1) * c] (dropping the terms that fall outside) to get each entry in O(1).
editorial: Handle the values one after another and keep ways[s], the number of ways to reach total s with the values processed so far. Adding a value c of which k copies exist, the new count is new[s] = ways[s] + ways[s - c] + ways[s - 2c] + ... + ways[s - kc], because the number of copies used can be anything from 0 to k. Computing each such sum from scratch costs O(k), so the whole table would cost O(n · amount · k).

The windows of consecutive entries overlap heavily. Compare new[s] with new[s - c]: they share every term except that new[s] gains ways[s] and loses ways[s - (k + 1)c]. So new[s] = new[s - c] + ways[s] - ways[s - (k + 1)c], where terms with a negative index are treated as 0. Every entry is O(1), for a total of O(n · amount) time and O(amount) space, all modulo 1,000,000,007.
